Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/running/bench/

# The Bench

The Bench is where you test and measure things before you wire them into an agent. Point it at a model to see how fast it answers, how it handles a prompt, and what it costs; point it at a published agent to run it with a real input and watch every step. It is the same tooling for a quick "does this work" check and a careful side-by-side comparison. (For trying a graph *while you are still building it*, the editor has its own [Test panel](../building/editor.md#testing-on-the-canvas) — no publish needed.)

There are two benches — one for models, one for agents — plus a small tester for MCP tools. All three share the same measurement and trace machinery.

## What you can bench

- **Models** — any registered model, across its modalities: chat and vision, embeddings, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech. Model testing goes **straight to your inference plane's data endpoints** — the raw prompt, image, or audio never passes through the control plane. Only the measured metrics are recorded afterwards.
- **Agents** — any [published agent](../building/saving-agents.md), run through the normal run path so you exercise the whole graph exactly as production would.
- **MCP tools** — a single registered tool, run standalone to check its shape and output.

## Benching a model

Open the [Registries](../models/index.md) page and press the **Bench** button on any model row (titled "Test & benchmark this model"). A modal opens titled `Bench · <logical id>`.

At the top, the model's capabilities are probed and shown as badges — its modalities, its maximum context, and an "approximate" marker when the probe is a static hint rather than a confirmed value. A **Warm** button preloads the engine so your first timing isn't skewed by the model loading; a warm that fails surfaces as an error rather than a mysterious slow run.

The panel you get below is chosen by the model's declared modalities:

| Modality | Panel | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| `chat` | Chat | A real multi-turn conversation with an optional system prompt. Vision rides here — image attach turns on when the model advertises vision. |
| `embeddings` | Embeddings | Embed one input, or two to see their cosine similarity. |
| `audio.transcription` | Speech-to-text | Record from the mic or attach an audio file; the transcript comes back as the reply. |
| `audio.speech` | Text-to-speech | Type text; the reply is a playable audio bubble. |

Image-generation models have no bench panel of their own — you exercise them from [New Chat](../chat/vision-and-images.md) instead.

### Tuning parameters

Each panel has a parameter form that is **schema-driven and capability-narrowed**: a parameter that needs a capability the model doesn't advertise is hidden, not greyed out, and every field has a `?` with help text. The chat form covers `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens` (placeholder `2048`), `stop`, `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `seed`, a **Reasoning** toggle, `reasoning_effort` (low/medium/high), `tool_choice`, and `response_format`. Embeddings, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech each have their own narrower set.

These are the same specs the [editor](../building/editor.md) uses to tune a node — so what you dial in on the Bench is exactly what you can set on a node or binding later.

### Reading the metrics

Every exchange is measured and the numbers show as badges. Which ones you see depend on the modality:

| Metric | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ttftMs` | TTFT | Time to the first visible answer token (thinking does not count — inline reasoning can't fake an early TTFT). |
| `totalMs` | Total | End-to-end time. |
| `tokensPerSec` | Throughput | Tokens per second over the post-TTFT generation window. |
| `promptTokens` / `completionTokens` | — | Token counts (completion falls back to a chunk count, clearly approximate, if the gateway reports no usage). |
| `cost` | Cost | USD, shown only when the gateway prices the call — absent for local engines. |
| `rtf` | Real-time factor | Speech-to-text: audio seconds ÷ processing seconds. |
| `ttfbMs` / `charsPerSec` | TTFB / Throughput | Text-to-speech: time to the first audio byte, and characters per second. |
| `latencyMs` | — | Image generation. |

### Saving, comparing, and presets

Three actions turn a one-off test into something reusable:

- **Save result** records this exchange's metrics to the control plane's bench store (`POST /bench/runs`). The server computes a `params_digest` (so two runs that differ by one parameter are distinct results) and an `output_digest` (a content fingerprint used for comparison **without** storing the raw output). The raw output is kept only if you opt in, and then only as a **local reference** on your own machine — never uploaded as a blob.
- **Compare** appears once you've saved two or more results in the modal. Pick an A and a B and you get per-metric deltas (B − A) and whether the outputs matched (digest equality — no payloads compared). Deltas are colored by direction: for throughput and real-time factor, higher is better; for latency and the rest, lower is better; zero is neutral. The compare list holds only results you recorded in the current modal session.
- **Save as preset** stores the current parameters as a named, modality-scoped snippet (`POST /bench/presets`). A preset is literal parameter values only — the name is never stored inside a graph, so it can't drift an agent's content hash. You can apply a preset to an agent later (below).

All of a model bench's raw traffic — `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, `/v1/images/generations` — goes directly to your inference plane. The control plane only ever sees the metrics and digests you save.

## Benching an agent

Open the Agents page (the grid of your [published agents](../building/saving-agents.md)) and press **Run** on an agent card — disabled until the agent has at least one published version. The agent bench modal opens. (The **Bench** button appears on *model* rows in [Registries](../models/index.md); an agent card uses **Run**.)

Pick a **Version** (it defaults to and follows the latest until you pin one), then give it an **Input**. The control follows the pinned version's input-node `modality` — a text box, a validated JSON editor, a microphone, an image attach, or a file picker — exactly as on the canvas and in chat; see [what the modality changes](../building/nodes/input-output.md#what-the-modality-changes). JSON is parsed loudly, so a malformed object tells you rather than failing silently, and a modality that needs an attachment keeps **Run** disabled until you stage one. A **JSON** option stays in the mode dropdown regardless, for the multi-input agents you address with `$in.in.<field>` (see [referencing inputs](../building/input-references.md)).

### Run vs Run durably

The **Run** control is a split button:

- **Run** launches a normal streaming run (`POST /agents/{id}/runs`). Reasoning arrives on its own channel and the answer streams token by token, exactly like chat.
- **Run durably** launches a checkpointed run on the [durable runtime](durable.md) (`POST /agents/{id}/durable-runs`). It returns a run id and the modal polls for the result — there is no token streaming, because a durable run journals results rather than streaming them. Use this to get crash-resumability.

Agents that contain `human`, `subgraph`, `loop`, or `map` nodes are **durable-only** — they can run only on the durable runtime, so the modal shows a single **Run durably** button for them.

!!! warning "Durable mode must be enabled"
    If the control plane isn't running in durable mode, a durable run returns a `durable_required` error and the modal shows: "The control-plane isn't running in durable mode — start it with `THEYGENT_DURABLE=1` to run durably." See [durable runs](durable.md).

### Reading an agent bench result

Once the stream ends, the canonical output is re-read from the persisted run row (a graph that ends at a tool or router emits no tokens — the stored output is what counts). The answer renders like a chat reply: a collapsible thinking block above a markdown bubble — or, for an `audio` or `image` output boundary, a player or the image itself rather than the artifact reference behind it. A **Stop** button aborts a streaming run mid-flight, and leaving the modal aborts it too.

Below the answer is the live [run waterfall](observability.md) alongside a read-only mini canvas of the pinned graph — hovering a node row in the waterfall flashes the matching node on the canvas, so you can see where the time went at a glance. If a durable run pauses at a human gate it shows a resume panel right there; the run buttons stay usable and the paused run remains visible under [Runs](index.md).

For agents that aren't durable-only, a **Chat** section lets you hold a real conversation with the agent — turns share session memory and record as a session under Recents, just like [chat](../chat/index.md). It reads the same boundary, so a voice agent gets the microphone composer here too.

### Applying a preset to an agent

If you saved parameter presets from a model bench, the agent bench offers **Apply a preset**: pick a saved preset and one of the agent's model bindings, and TheYgent writes the preset's literal parameters into that binding and publishes a **new agent version** through the registry. Each preset's modality is shown beside its name so you can tell which binding it belongs on; the preset name never enters the graph — only its values do, so the new version's [content hash](../concepts/versioning.md) reflects real content.

## Testing an MCP tool

The [MCP](../building/nodes/mcp.md) page has a **tool tester** for exercising one registered tool in isolation. Pick a connected server, name a tool, and send it either an uploaded image (under a configurable argument name) or free-form JSON arguments. It composes a throwaway `input → mcp_tool → output` graph and runs it through the normal run path — no special execution route — so what you see is exactly what an agent would get. Structured detections (for example bounding boxes from a vision tool) draw over the image; raw output shows below.

## Where results are stored

Saved model-bench results, presets, and any test suites live in the control plane's Postgres database (the bench tables), alongside your runs and agents. What is stored is deliberately lightweight:

- **Metrics and digests**, not raw outputs. The `output_digest` lets comparisons check whether two outputs matched without keeping the text.
- **Raw output only on opt-in**, and then only as a **local reference** in your own trust domain — TheYgent never uploads the generated text, image, or audio.
- Bench records carry the coordinates you'd expect for later analysis: `target_kind` (`model` or `agent`), `modality`, `logical_id`, `binding`, the `params` and their digest, the `metrics`, the `output_digest`, and a `run_id`.

Saved results are readable through the API (`GET /bench/runs`, filterable by `logical_id`, `agent_id`, `suite_id`, or `case_id`) and comparable in-modal. Suites of golden cases and assertions exist in the API for future use, but there is no page for them yet — recording results, in-modal compare, and presets are what the interface surfaces today.

## Works well with

- [Installing local models](../models/installing.md) — get a model into your registry so it has a Bench button.
- [Remote models](../models/remote.md) — register a hosted, OpenAI-compatible model to bench (and to see a cost figure).
- [Observability](observability.md) — the run waterfall the agent bench embeds.
- [Durable runs](durable.md) — what "Run durably" does and why some agents require it.
- [Drafts & publishing](../building/saving-agents.md) — creating the versions the agent bench runs and the presets it applies.

---

Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/ai-gateway/

# AI Gateway

The AI Gateway sits between **Claude Code** — the CLI, IDE extensions, and the desktop app — and
the Anthropic API. It records what each exchange cost, what it would have cost if subagents and
cold-cache turns had run on a cheaper model, and why each request was or wasn't a candidate — and,
once you choose to, it **routes** them there: to a cheaper Anthropic model, or to
[models you run yourself](local-models.md). You see where your team's model spend goes, per day,
model, developer and session, before you move anything.

!!! note "Observe first, then route"
    In **observer** mode every request reaches Anthropic exactly as Claude Code sent it; the
    gateway reports what routing *would* save. When those figures convince you, an admin switches
    to **router** mode, and the saving becomes real: a subagent asking for Opus 5.5 runs on
    Sonnet 5.5, for example. Only the model changes — never the prompt — and a model that refuses
    a request hands it back to the one Claude Code asked for before Claude Code notices. The one
    setting the setup adds that changes Claude Code's own behavior, [tool search](setup.md#why-each-setting),
    turns back on what a custom gateway address otherwise turns off.

## What you get

- **Spend and what routing would save — or saved** — per day, request class (main
  conversation, subagents, compaction, side requests), model, client, developer and session. See
  [Reports & policy](reports.md).
- **Session timelines** — every request of a Claude Code session in order, with what the
  policy would have done and the reasons, in plain words.
- **Setup warnings** — for example, Claude Code sending every tool's definition with every
  request because tool search is off, which can multiply input tokens several times.
- **Subscription seats** — for developers on a claude.ai plan, how much of the plan's
  five-hour and weekly allowance their traffic used.
- **Local models** — a share of the work, per kind of request, answered by models on your
  inference plane at no API spend, each measured on your own traffic first. See
  [Local models](local-models.md).

## What it sees, and what leaves it

The gateway relays prompts, code, model responses and credentials, so it runs **where you run
it** — your machine or your cluster — in the same trust domain as Claude Code. It never writes a
prompt or a response anywhere, and never stores a credential except an organization key you give
it.

What it sends to the control plane is **metadata only**: timings, model names, token counts and
costs, the routing decision and its reasons, Claude Code's session and agent ids, and the kind of
each request. Never prompt or response text. Everyone sees their own records in full; admins see
everyone's; other roles see organization totals without individual detail.

## Personal or team

| | Personal | Team |
|---|---|---|
| Who it serves | You, on your own machine | Every developer who points Claude Code at it |
| Listens on | Loopback only (`127.0.0.1`) | Any address you choose |
| Identifies callers by | Nobody — it is yours | Each developer's **gateway key** (`tyg_…`) |
| Billing | Your own Claude login or API key | Each developer's own credential, or the organization's key |
| Records | Kept locally; read them with the `report` command, or attach it to the control plane | Sent to the control plane: the **AI Gateway** page |

[Running the gateway](running.md) covers both, on a machine, in Docker Compose, and in
Kubernetes.

## Observer, router and passthrough

An admin chooses the gateway's **mode** on the AI Gateway **Settings** tab:

- **Observer** records every exchange — its cost and what routing would have done — without
  changing it.
- **Router** records every exchange and applies the routing decisions: routed requests run on the
  target model — a cheaper Anthropic model with the rest of the request exactly as Claude Code
  sent it, or a [local model](local-models.md). A target that refuses
  a request sends it back to the requested model, unseen, and that conversation stays there until
  its cache goes cold. Switching back to observer stops routing within one heartbeat (30 seconds).
- **Passthrough** forwards traffic without recording anything.

A gateway attached to the control plane forwards in passthrough until an admin saves a
configuration: your organization's traffic is recorded only once someone chose to record it. A
personal gateway on its own records from the start.

## Try it on your own machine

A personal gateway needs no keys and no setup beyond Claude Code's settings:

1. **Start TheYgent** with `make up` ([Running TheYgent](../getting-started/running.md)). The
   gateway listens on `127.0.0.1:8082`.
2. **Point Claude Code at it**, in the shell you start Claude Code from:

    ```bash
    export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL='http://localhost:8082'
    export CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS='1'
    export ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH='true'
    ```

3. **Work as usual.** Your own Claude login or API key goes through the gateway unchanged.
4. **Read the report** — what your traffic cost, and what routing would save:

    ```bash
    uv run --package theygent-ai-gateway theygent-ai-gateway report --since 24h
    ```

5. **To see it on the AI Gateway page, and to route**, attach the gateway to the control plane
   with a service key ([Running the gateway](running.md#attach-it-to-the-control-plane)). Then
   save a configuration on **AI Gateway → Settings**: observer mode to record, router mode to
   route.

## Getting started with a team

1. **Run a gateway** — [Running the gateway](running.md).
2. **Turn recording on** — an admin opens **AI Gateway → Settings** and saves the configuration
   with **Observer** selected.
3. **Set up Claude Code** — each developer opens **AI Gateway → Setup & keys**, creates a gateway
   key, and copies the setup for their terminal, IDE or desktop app —
   [Set up Claude Code](setup.md).
4. **Work as usual** — then watch **Overview**, **Report** and **Sessions**.
5. **Route** — when the Report's saving is one you want, an admin selects **Router** on the
   Settings tab (with a subagent target such as `claude-sonnet-5-5`). The Report then shows what
   routing *saved*, against what the same traffic would have cost on the models Claude Code asked
   for.

## The AI Gateway page

| Tab | Who | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **Overview** | everyone | The mode, the configuration version, each gateway instance's health (online, running the latest configuration, upstream reachable, records waiting to export) |
| **Report** | everyone | Spend, what it would have cost with routing, the saving, spend by day, breakdowns, seats, setup warnings |
| **Sessions** | everyone | Claude Code sessions, most recently active first, and each one's timeline of requests and decisions |
| **Setup & keys** | everyone | How you are billed, your gateway keys, and copy-ready setups per client |
| **Catalog** | admins | Kinds of side requests Claude Code sends (titles, suggestions, checks) and what routing may do with each |
| **Settings** | admins | The configuration and its history, the organization's Anthropic key, developers' billing, service keys |

## Related pages

- [Set up Claude Code](setup.md) — the settings, per client, and why each one is there.
- [Reports & policy](reports.md) — reading the figures, and how the policy decides.
- [Local models](local-models.md) — sending work to models you run, measured first.
- [Running the gateway](running.md) — run modes, the organization's key, errors.
- [Environment variables](../reference/environment.md#ai-gateway) — the gateway's settings.

Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/ai-gateway/setup/

# Set up Claude Code

Pointing Claude Code at the AI Gateway is a handful of environment settings. The **Setup & keys**
tab on the AI Gateway page builds them for you — with your key filled in, right after you create
it — so this page explains what they are and why each one is there.

## Before you start

- **The gateway's address.** By default `http://localhost:8082`. If your team runs a shared
  gateway, use its address; the Setup & keys tab lets you set the address its snippets use.
- **A gateway key** (team gateways only). Create one on **Setup & keys → New key**. It is shown
  **once**, in the dialog that creates it, together with setups that already contain it. A
  gateway key identifies you to the gateway and opens nothing else in TheYgent; revoke it there
  when a machine is retired.
- **How you are billed.** An admin sets it per developer (**Settings → Developers**):

    | Billing | Your traffic reaches Anthropic with | Your gateway key travels as |
    |---|---|---|
    | **Your own Claude login or API key** | your claude.ai subscription or your own API key, as today | a header of its own (`X-TheYgent-Gateway-Key`) |
    | **The organization's key** | the organization's Anthropic key, which the gateway adds in place of yours | your only credential (`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`) |

    The Setup & keys tab shows which one applies to you and builds the matching setup.

## Terminal and IDEs

For the CLI — and IDE extensions launched from a terminal that has these set — export them in
your shell profile. Billed to your own credential:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL='http://localhost:8082'
export ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS='X-TheYgent-Gateway-Key: tyg_…your gateway key'
export CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS='1'
export ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH='true'
```

Billed to the organization's key, the gateway key *is* your credential:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL='http://localhost:8082'
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN='tyg_…your gateway key'
export CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS='1'
export ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH='true'
```

On a **personal** gateway there is no key: set `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and the last two lines.

## `settings.json`

The same settings work as the `env` block of `~/.claude/settings.json`, which every Claude Code
session reads, however it was started:

```json
{
  "env": {
    "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "http://localhost:8082",
    "ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS": "X-TheYgent-Gateway-Key: tyg_…your gateway key",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS": "1",
    "ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH": "true"
  }
}
```

## The desktop app

The desktop app ignores `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `settings.json`; it reaches a gateway only
through its own third-party inference settings, which carry an API key and never a claude.ai
login. So it works through the gateway **for developers billed to the organization's key**:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Inference provider | Gateway |
| Gateway base URL | the gateway's address |
| API key | your gateway key |
| Tool search | On |

Developers on their own claude.ai login keep using the CLI and IDEs through the gateway.

## For admins: managed settings

The **Managed settings** view on Setup & keys gives the `env` block for everyone at once — the
gateway's address and the two flags, **never a key**; each developer adds their own. Distribute
it the way you distribute Claude Code's managed settings today.

## Why each setting

- **`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`** sends Claude Code's model traffic to the gateway instead of straight
  to Anthropic.
- **`CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1`** makes Claude Code label each request: the main
  conversation, a subagent, compaction, a side request, and the session and agent it belongs
  to. Without the labels the gateway cannot tell those apart, so no request is a routing
  candidate. The Report warns when they are missing.
- **`CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW`** (in a shell) or **`autoCompactWindow`** (in a settings
  file) appears only when the gateway serves main conversations on a local model. Claude Code
  compacts by the context window of the model it asked for, 1 million tokens for current models;
  this tells it to compact while the conversation still fits the local model. See
  [Local models](local-models.md#5-for-the-main-conversation-update-claude-codes-setup).
- **`ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true`** keeps MCP tool search on. Claude Code turns it **off for any
  custom base URL**, and then every request carries the full definition of every connected tool.
  In one measurement with many connectors loaded, a one-line prompt went from about 28,000 to
  184,000 input tokens — 6.5 times as many. The Report flags this as *tool search is off*.

## Claude Code's own cost display

Claude Code prices every token at the model it **asked for**. In observer mode that is also the
model that answered, so Claude Code's figures and the gateway's agree (at list prices; the gateway
also applies any contracted rates an admin entered).

In **router** mode, routed requests run on a cheaper model, but Claude Code still files and prices
them under the model it asked for. Its own cost figures overstate spend: the session cost, the
usage summary, a status line that shows cost, and the SDK's `total_cost_usd`. For example, one
Explore subagent task cost $0.16 on Opus 5.5 and $0.08 on Sonnet 5.5, with near-identical token
counts. Route that subagent to Sonnet and Claude Code still shows about $0.16 for it. On the AI
Gateway **Report**, its spend is about $0.08, and $0.16 appears as *without routing*.

The token counts still agree. Claude Code's per-model usage matches the Report grouped by **model
requested**, and **served model** shows where the tokens actually went. The Report is the figure to
trust for cost. On a subscription, dollar figures are the API-equivalent value of the traffic, not
a bill; the Report shows plan usage separately.

## Check that it works

1. Run any Claude Code prompt.
2. On **AI Gateway → Sessions**, your session appears with its requests, once the gateway is in
   observer mode (records reach the page within a few seconds).
3. If Claude Code reports an error from the gateway instead, the message names what is missing
   — see [errors the gateway returns](running.md#errors-the-gateway-returns).

## Related pages

- [AI Gateway](index.md) — what the gateway does and what leaves it.
- [Reports & policy](reports.md) — what the figures mean.
- [Running the gateway](running.md) — starting one, and its errors.

---

Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/ai-gateway/reports/

# Reports & policy

What the AI Gateway page's figures mean, how the routing policy decides what moves, and how admins
tune it. In observer mode the gateway only records each decision; in router mode it also applies
it — changing nothing but the model.

## The Report tab

The report covers the last week unless you pick another range. Admins start on everyone's
traffic; everyone else on their own (and can switch to organization totals).

| Tile | Means |
|---|---|
| **Spend** | What the traffic cost, at list prices plus any contracted rates an admin entered. Once the gateway routes, its hint shows what the same traffic would have cost *without routing* — on the models Claude Code asked for |
| **With routing** | What it costs with the policy's decisions applied: a request the gateway routed costs what it cost, one it only would have routed costs the target's price, everything else as it ran |
| **Saving** | Without routing minus with routing: what routing saved (router mode) or would save (observer mode), and its share |
| **Calls** | API calls, how many were routed, how many would have been, and how many could have been answered by a local model instead |

Below them: spend by day (the full bar is what each day cost as requested, the filled part with
routing; the gap is the saving), and a
breakdown you can group by request class, client, the model Claude Code requested, the model that
served it, the routing decision or its reason, the model a shadow run ran on — and, where you may
see individuals, by developer or session. Grouping by requested model matches Claude Code's own usage summary, which files every
token under the model it asked for.

**Shadow runs.** A saving is an estimate: it assumes the target would have written as much as
the model Claude Code asked for. Shadow runs check it. After a request that routing would have sent
elsewhere, the gateway sends a copy to that target; after a request in a local dial's *trial* (see
Settings below), it sends a copy to the local model. Claude Code never sees the copy, and it never
delays Claude Code's answer. The **Shadow runs** table shows, per model, how many copies ran,
how many of their answers routing could have used, and how much the target wrote compared with
the model Claude Code asked for. For agent turns (subagents and the main conversation) it also
shows how often the target picked the same next action as the real reply: the same tool first, or
the answer where the reply answered. That is the measure to watch before trusting a local model
with agent work. It also shows what the copies cost, which is kept apart from the spend above. The
Sessions timeline shows the shadow run under each request that had one, a trial named as such.

**Subscription seats.** For developers on a claude.ai plan, the dollar figures are the
API-equivalent value of their traffic, not a bill. The seats table shows each developer's latest
reading of the plan's five-hour and weekly allowance and how much of it was used in the range.

**Setup warnings** appear above the figures when the traffic shows a problem, each with its fix:

| Warning | Fix |
|---|---|
| Tool search is off — every tool's definition went with every request | Set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true` (desktop app: tool search on) |
| Claude Code is not labelling its requests | Set `CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1` |
| Unknown request classes | A newer Claude Code than this gateway knows: update TheYgent |
| No price known for a model | An admin adds its rates under **Settings → Contracted prices** |

## The Sessions tab

Sessions are listed most recently active first — yours, or everyone's for admins. Open one for its
timeline: each request in order with its offset from the session start, its class (main,
subagent, compaction, auxiliary), the agent type for subagents, the model requested and the one
that served it, tokens, cost, errors, and the decision — *stays*; *routed →* a target, with what that
saved against the requested model (router mode); or *would route →* a target, with what that would
have cost (observer mode). Every reason is a short label; hover it for the explanation. A few of
them:

| Reason | Means |
|---|---|
| subagent spawn | A subagent starts with an empty cache, so moving it costs nothing extra |
| cold cache | The main conversation's cache is cold (its start, after compaction, or expired) |
| mid-conversation | Inside one prompt's tool loop: a conversation never switches mid-turn |
| warm cache | Moving would throw away a warm cache and pay to rebuild it |
| follows cache | The conversation keeps the model its cache is on until the cache goes cold |
| switch pays | Staying would cost at least the configured margin times rebuilding the cache elsewhere |
| no target set | The configuration names no target for this kind of request |
| target can't take it | The target model would reject this request's shape |
| target not cheaper | The target doesn't cost less than the model Claude Code asked for |
| unreviewed kind | A side request whose kind an admin has not reviewed in the Catalog |
| local share | The conversation is in the share its kind sends to a [local model](local-models.md) |
| no local model fits | In the local share, but no listed local model can take this request (tool calls, images or prompt size) |
| outgrew local model | The conversation grew past its local model: it moved to a larger listed one, or to Anthropic when none can take it |
| target refused | The target, or the local model, could not take the request: it went to the model Claude Code asked for, unseen |

## How the policy decides

Prompt caches belong to one model, so moving a conversation mid-stream throws a warm cache away
and pays to rebuild it. The policy therefore only considers a move where the cache is cold anyway:

- **A subagent, when it starts.** Its cache is empty either way — the clearest saving. In
  measurements, the same exploration subagent cost about half as much on Sonnet 5.5 as on
  Opus 5.5.
- **The main conversation, at a cold point** — its start, after compaction, or after its cache
  expired — and only if the configuration names a main target.
- **Then it stays where its cache is.** Every later request — the tool loop, and new prompts while
  the cache is warm — follows the same decision until the next cold point (*follows cache*), so a
  conversation never changes model mid-turn, and a routed one isn't pulled back to the requested
  model either. A warm move happens only where staying would cost at least the **warm switch
  margin** times rebuilding the cache on the other model (*switch pays*). If Claude Code switches
  model itself, the policy decides afresh.

Some traffic never moves: Claude Code's quota check, side requests that ride the main
conversation's cache, auto mode's safety checks, and side requests of a kind nobody has reviewed.
Compaction reads the main conversation's cache, so it moves only with the conversation: it runs
on the model the conversation is on — the one asked for, a cheaper one, or a local one. And a target must accept the request: Sonnet 5.5
takes Claude Code's requests to Opus 5.5 as they are; Haiku 4.5 rejects them, so a move to it is
turned down as *target can't take it*. A target must also cost less, at your contracted prices
where you set them. A request that already asks for a cheaper model, such as a subagent on
Haiku 4.5, or for a model with no known price, stays as *target not cheaper*.

**Estimates.** A "with routing" figure assumes the target model would have used the same number
of tokens. Models differ in how much they write, so treat savings as estimates; the actual
figures are exact.

**Archived days.** Requests older than the retention period (90 days by default) are archived:
the Report reads those days from daily totals, so every figure and grouping stays the same. Its
footer says from which day that applies. Setup warnings, seat readings and the prices used cover
only the days still kept in detail. A Sessions timeline lists only the requests still kept in
detail, and its totals still count every request.

**Prices.** Figures use Anthropic's published list prices. The Report's footer names the date
they were read (*Prices: 2026-10-11*), and TheYgent checks for changes every week. Requests in
Claude Code's fast mode are priced at fast-mode rates. A model priced by prompt length, such as
Haiku 5.5, is priced at its higher rates for a long prompt. Where your organization pays other
rates, an admin enters them under **Settings → Contracted prices**.

## Catalog (admins)

Claude Code also sends small **side requests** — session titles, suggestions, checks. The Catalog
lists each kind it has seen, told apart by the shape of the request, with how often it was seen,
the Claude Code versions that sent it, and its status:

| Status | Routing may |
|---|---|
| unreviewed | do nothing — it passes through untouched until someone decides |
| observe only | record and report it, never route it |
| cheaper model | send it to the configuration's subagent target |
| local model | answer it with the configuration's local model |
| never route | do nothing — it always stays on the model Claude Code asked for |

Kinds the gateway recognises by their shape come with a **suggestion** — the quota check and
side requests riding the main conversation's cache: *never route*; the session title: *local
model* — which you can apply in one click or override with **Review**. A suggestion is only that:
the status is your decision, and saving one creates a new configuration version.

In router mode, a *local model* side request goes to a model on your inference plane, the
**Side requests** dial's (see [Local models](local-models.md)). Claude Code gets the local
model's answer in the form the Anthropic API would have given it, but only after the gateway has
checked it: for a session title, JSON with a `title`. A request the local model cannot take goes to
the model Claude Code asked for, marked *target refused*, and Claude Code never sees the
difference. That covers a request carrying something that doesn't translate (a document, for
example), an error, no answer in time, an answer of the wrong shape, or no inference plane
running. A local answer costs no API spend; its *without routing* figure is an estimate, counted
with the local model's tokens.

## Settings (admins)

- **Mode** — observer, router or passthrough (see
  [AI Gateway](index.md#observer-router-and-passthrough)). Saving refuses a target no Claude Code
  request could go to — a model the gateway has no data for, or one that rejects Claude Code's
  requests, such as Haiku 4.5.
- **Routing targets** — the Anthropic model a subagent could start on (for example
  `claude-sonnet-5-5`), the model for the main conversation at cold points (empty: never
  considered), and the local model for side requests the Catalog allows to run locally (a
  [logical model id](../concepts/models-and-engines.md)).
- **Local models** — the models on your inference plane that may take Claude Code's work, listed
  small to large, each with its context size, the most it may write in a turn, whether it follows
  tool calls and takes images, and optionally what it costs to run.
  Beside each one is what the last week shows: the requests it served, and how often it picked the
  same next action as Claude. Then one dial per kind of request (side requests, subagents, the
  main conversation), each a **share** served locally, a **trial** measured locally while
  Anthropic answers, and the **model** (or "smallest that fits"). How to set them, and their
  limits: [Local models](local-models.md).
- **Warm switch margin** — a conversation whose cache is warm moves only where staying would cost
  at least this many times rebuilding its cache on the other model (at least 1). Cache reads cost
  a fraction of cache writes, so in practice warm conversations stay put.
- **Shadow runs** — which targets get shadow runs (see the Report tab above).
    - *Local model* is on by default. It costs no API spend, only the local model's time. (A
      dial's trial is its own choice and runs whatever this says.)
    - *Cloud targets* are off by default, because each copy is a real API call. Cloud shadow runs
      use only the organization's key (on a personal gateway, your own API key), never a
      subscription seat's login or a developer's own key. They stop for the day at the **budget**
      (per gateway instance, counted from its last restart), and pause for ten minutes when the
      target's rate limit runs low.
- **Contracted prices** — per-model rates (USD per million tokens: input, output, 5-minute and
  1-hour cache writes, cache reads) where yours differ from list price.

Every save creates a new, immutable **version**; gateways pick it up at their next heartbeat
(every 30 seconds by default). The **History** lists every version; loading an older one starts
an edit from it, and saving makes it the newest. If someone else saved meanwhile, the page keeps
your edit and asks before replacing theirs — their Catalog reviews are kept either way.

The same tab holds the [organization's Anthropic key](running.md#the-organizations-key),
**Developers** (who pays for each developer's traffic) and the gateways' **service keys**
([Running the gateway](running.md#attach-it-to-the-control-plane)).

## Related pages

- [AI Gateway](index.md) — what the gateway does and what leaves it.
- [Set up Claude Code](setup.md) — the settings the warnings refer to.
- [Local models](local-models.md) — the local dials, trials and their limits.
- [Running the gateway](running.md) — the command-line report for a personal gateway.

Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/ai-gateway/local-models/

# Local models

In router mode, the AI Gateway can answer some of Claude Code's work with models you run on your
[inference plane](../concepts/models-and-engines.md), instead of the Anthropic API. A request a
local model answers costs no API spend. How much goes local is your choice, per kind of request,
and you measure a model on your own traffic before it serves any.

!!! note "Measure before you serve"
    A small model follows Claude Code's agent work poorly. In one measurement, a 4-billion-parameter
    model picked the same next step as Claude on 1 real exploration turn in 6. A larger model does
    better, but only your own traffic can say by how much. So every agent share starts at 0%, and a
    **trial** measures a model on conversations Anthropic still answers.

## How it works

Each kind of request has a **dial** on **AI Gateway → Settings → Local models**:

| Dial | Default | What goes local |
|---|---|---|
| Side requests | 100% | The kinds of side request (session titles, for example) an admin reviewed *local model* in the [Catalog](reports.md#catalog-admins) |
| Subagents | 0% | A share of subagents, from their first request to their last. You can limit it to some agent types, such as `Explore` |
| Main conversation | 0% | A share of conversations, from their start or their last compaction |

Each dial has three settings:

- **Share.** The percentage of conversations served by a local model. A conversation is in or out
  of the share the same way every time, and only where its prompt cache is cold anyway: when a
  subagent starts, when a conversation starts, or after compaction. It then stays on that model for
  its whole task, so a conversation never changes model mid-turn. A conversation already running
  when you raise a share moves at its next cold point.
- **Trial.** A further percentage of conversations, just above the share. Anthropic still answers
  them. Afterwards the gateway sends each of their requests to the local model and records whether
  it picked the **same next action** as the real answer: the same tool first, or answering where
  the real answer answered. A trial costs no API spend, works in router mode too, and never delays
  anyone: a request a local model is serving always comes first, and a trial running then is
  dropped. Raising the share by the trial serves exactly the conversations that were tried. The
  share and the trial add up to 100% at most.
- **Model.** A listed model, or *smallest that fits*: the first model in the list that can take the
  request. A subagent or main-conversation turn needs a model that follows tool calls. A request
  with images needs one that takes images. Every model needs the prompt to fit within its context.

**A conversation that outgrows its model moves up.** When a conversation's prompt no longer fits
its local model, it moves to the next larger listed model that can take it, marked *outgrew local
model*, and stays there. Only when no listed model can take it does it go to Anthropic, which reads
the whole history without a cache, and stays there until its next cold point.

When a local model can't take a request for another reason, Anthropic answers it before Claude
Code sees anything. That covers an error, no answer in time, or an answer that isn't usable. The
request is marked *target refused*, and the conversation stays with Anthropic until its next cold
point.

## Set it up

### 1. Run a model

Register the model on the inference plane under a [logical model id](../concepts/models-and-engines.md),
such as `coder-medium`. It can be:

- a model you [install and run locally](../models/installing.md) (llama.cpp or MLX), or
- a model served elsewhere, on your own GPU servers for example, registered as a
  [remote, OpenAI-compatible model](../models/remote.md): its URL and, if it needs one, its key.

For subagents and the main conversation, choose a model that follows tool calls well and has a
large context: Claude Code's subagent turns carry about 7,000 to 20,000 tokens, and a main
conversation grows well beyond that.

The gateway reaches the inference plane at `THEYGENT_INFERENCE_PLANE_URL`
(`http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1` by default). A gateway on another machine needs that address.

### 2. List it

On **AI Gateway → Settings → Local models**, choose **Add a local model** and fill in:

| Field | Set it to |
|---|---|
| Logical id | The id you registered on the inference plane |
| Context (tokens) | The context the model is served with: the gateway never sends a larger prompt |
| Max output (tokens) | The most it may write in one subagent or main-conversation turn (16,384 unless you change it). Raise it for a large model that writes whole files |
| Tool calls | Ticked if it follows tool calls well enough for agent work |
| Images | Ticked if it takes images |
| Cost | Optional: what running it costs, in USD per million input and output tokens (your hardware, power or rental, spread over what it serves). Leave both empty and its answers count as costing nothing |

List models small to large: *smallest that fits* picks the first that can take a request. A very
small model for side requests and a medium one for agent work is a common pair.

### 3. Measure it with a trial

Set a trial on the dial you want to grow, for example **Subagents: share 0%, trial 20%**, with
**Only these agent types** set to `Explore` to start with the simplest subagents. Save. Then read
the evidence:

- **Settings → Local models** shows, beside each model, the requests it served in the last week
  and how often it picked the same next action.
- **Report → Shadow runs** shows the same per model: how many copies ran, how many answers were
  usable, the *same next action* rate, and how much it wrote against the model Claude Code asked
  for.
- **Sessions** shows each tried request with *Local trial on …* under it, and the verdict.

Trials are samples. A gateway runs one local trial at a time, and a request that finishes while
one is running is not tried. A busy team therefore has a fraction of its turns tried.

### 4. Raise the share

When the *same next action* rate is one you trust, move the trial into the share: **share 20%,
trial 20%** serves the conversations you measured and starts measuring the next ones. Raise it
step by step. The Report then counts what the local model served as routed, at no API spend, and
shows it against what the same work would have cost on the model Claude Code asked for.

### 5. For the main conversation: update Claude Code's setup

Claude Code decides when to compact a conversation from the context window of the model it asked
for, which is 1 million tokens for current models behind a gateway. A local model holds far less,
so left alone, a long conversation would outgrow it. Once the **Main conversation** dial has a
share, the setups on **Setup & keys** also tell Claude Code to compact sooner: at three quarters of
the context of the largest local model a main conversation can reach (for example 196,000 tokens
for a 262,144-token model). The compaction then runs on the local model too, and the conversation
never has to leave it. The Settings tab shows the value under the dial.

Developers pick it up by copying their setup again (it adds `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` to
the shell setup, and `autoCompactWindow` to `settings.json`), or from the managed settings an admin
distributes. Claude Code compacts no earlier than 100,000 tokens, so a model for the main
conversation needs about 125,000 tokens of context or more; the Setup & keys and Settings tabs say
when the listed ones fall short.

## What always stays with Anthropic

Some requests never go to a local model, whatever the dials say:

- Claude Code's quota check, auto mode's safety checks, side requests that reuse the main
  conversation's cache, and side-request kinds nobody has reviewed.
- **Compaction of a conversation Anthropic serves.** Compaction reads the conversation's cache, so
  it runs where the conversation runs: a conversation on a local model is compacted by that model.
- **Requests that can't be translated faithfully**: documents such as PDFs, Anthropic's server
  tools (web search, code execution) and their results, and images for a model that doesn't take
  them.
- **Token counting** and **model listing**.

The gateway therefore still needs an Anthropic credential: local models extend it, they don't
replace it.

## Limits to know

- **Answers have time limits.** A local model's answer must start within 15 seconds, plus the time
  to read the prompt, or Anthropic answers instead. Reading is counted at 100 tokens a second, or at
  the model's own speed where the gateway has measured it slower: it measures each model on the
  answers it serves, and a model reads a long conversation much slower than a short one. A long
  prompt is therefore waited for at least as long as Claude Code itself waits. An answer that
  opens with a tool call is held back until the call is whole, so Anthropic can still step in: the
  model may pause no more than 30 seconds while writing it, and the call must be whole within 5
  minutes of the request. A large file written steadily is waited for; a model that stalls is
  not. Once an answer has gone out, Claude Code gets it to the end. A side request's answer is
  checked whole, so it must be complete within 30 seconds plus the reading time.
- **Claude Code waits about five minutes for an answer to start.** Its stream watchdogs give up
  on a response that sends nothing for that long, and then retry the request. A local model that
  needs longer to read a prompt (a long conversation on modest hardware, after a compaction for
  example) causes that: the engine usually finishes reading meanwhile, so the retry is answered
  quickly from its cache, at no API spend, but the developer waits. To have Claude Code wait
  instead, raise `CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (up to 30 minutes), set `API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT`
  to `0`, and raise `API_TIMEOUT_MS` (see Claude Code's
  [environment variables](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars)). A faster engine is the better
  fix: a model that reads a few thousand tokens a second never comes near it.
- **Answers have length limits.** A subagent or main-conversation turn can write up to the model's
  **max output** (16,384 tokens unless you raise it), and a side request up to 4,096.
- **Claude Code compacts by the model it asked for**, unless its setup says otherwise: see
  [step 5](#5-for-the-main-conversation-update-claude-codes-setup). A developer still on an older
  setup compacts late, and their long conversations move to larger models, or to Anthropic.
- **Prompt sizes are estimated.** The gateway counts about 2.75 bytes of Claude Code's request per
  token, a little more than real sessions use, so it moves a conversation slightly before its model
  is full rather than after.
- **Local compute is priced only if you price it.** Without a **cost**, the Report counts a local
  answer as costing nothing, and the saving it shows is larger than your real saving if your
  models run on hardware you pay for. With one, local answers, trials and what routing would cost
  in observer mode are all counted at it.
- **Concurrency is the engine's.** Each developer's requests reach the model as they come. An engine
  serving one request at a time makes the others wait, and a request that waits past the time limit
  goes to Anthropic. For a team, serve the model with an engine that handles many requests at once
  (vLLM is experimental), or give a llama.cpp model several slots with its `parallel` setting
  ([engine settings](../models/engines.md)). The slots share the context, so raise `ctxSize` with
  them.

## Send as much as you can to one large model

For a team running a large model on its own servers:

1. Register it on the inference plane as a remote model, and list it with its real context and
   **Tool calls** ticked. Give the main conversation a model with a large context: 128K tokens
   at the very least, more is better.
2. Measure it first: a trial on **Subagents**, then on **Main conversation**.
3. Set **Subagents** and **Main conversation** to a 100% share, and review the side-request kinds
   you want local as *local model* in the Catalog.
4. Run in **Router** mode, and have every developer take the updated setup from **Setup & keys**
   (or distribute the managed settings), so Claude Code compacts while conversations still fit.

Every subagent and main-conversation turn then goes to the local model, except what [stays with
Anthropic](#what-always-stays-with-anthropic) and what falls back under the
[limits above](#limits-to-know). Watch **Report → Calls**, and the *outgrew local model* and
*target refused* reasons on the Sessions tab, to see how much still reaches Anthropic, and why.

## Related pages

- [Reports & policy](reports.md) — the figures, the reasons, and the rest of the Settings tab.
- [Installing local models](../models/installing.md) and [Remote models](../models/remote.md) —
  getting a model onto the inference plane.
- [Engines](../models/engines.md) — engine settings, such as parallel slots.

# Running the gateway

The AI Gateway is the fourth TheYgent service, on port **8082**. It runs the same way as the
others — on a machine with `make up`, in Docker Compose, or in Kubernetes — and in one of two
[modes](index.md#personal-or-team): **personal** (yours, on loopback, no keys) or **team** (shared,
developers identified by gateway keys).

## On your machine

`make up` starts the gateway with the other services, configured by your `.env`. As shipped in
`.env.example` it is a **personal gateway**: it listens on `127.0.0.1:8082`, forwards your own
Claude login or API key, and records from the start, locally.

Read what it recorded with the report command:

```bash
uv run --package theygent-ai-gateway theygent-ai-gateway report --since 24h
```

`--by class,client,model` (also `session`, `served-model`, `decision`, `reason`, `shadow-model`) picks the
groupings, `--since`/`--until` take `30m`, `24h`, `7d`, `2w` or a date, and `--json` prints JSON.
It computes the same totals as the Report tab, with the same setup warnings.

### Attach it to the control plane

To see a gateway on the **AI Gateway** page, it reports to the control plane with a **service
key**:

1. An admin mints one under **AI Gateway → Settings → Service keys → New service key**. It is
   shown once, beside the line to paste into `.env`.
2. In `.env`, set:

    ```bash
    THEYGENT_CONTROL_PLANE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080
    THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_SERVICE_KEY=tygs_…
    ```

3. `make restart`. The gateway appears on the **Overview** within one heartbeat (30 seconds).

Attached, a gateway forwards without recording until an admin saves a configuration in observer
mode — see [Settings](reports.md#settings-admins).

### Serve other machines (team mode)

A personal gateway accepts requests without a key, so it refuses to listen beyond loopback. To
serve your team from this machine, attach it as above and add:

```bash
THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_AUTH_MODE=team
THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_HOST=0.0.0.0
```

Every request then needs a developer's gateway key; developers create theirs on **Setup & keys**
and point Claude Code at `http://<this machine>:8082`. If the interface is served from another
origin than `http://localhost:5174`, add it to `THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_ADMIN_ORIGINS` so the
Settings tab can reach the gateway.

## Docker Compose

The containerized gateway always runs in team mode, so it starts only with a service key. Bring
the stack up, mint a service key as an admin, put it in `.env` as
`THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_SERVICE_KEY`, then:

```bash
docker compose --profile gateway up -d
```

It publishes `:8082`, keeps its state in a Docker volume, and waits for open streams to finish
when it stops. The organization's key can come from `.env`
(`THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_ORG_API_KEY`) or from the Settings tab.

## Kubernetes

`kubectl apply -k deploy/k8s` creates the gateway with the rest of the stack, and it waits until
its Secret exists. Mint a service key as an admin, then:

```bash
kubectl -n theygent create secret generic theygent-ai-gateway \
  --from-literal=THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_SERVICE_KEY=tygs_… \
  --from-literal=THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_ORG_API_KEY=sk-ant-…   # optional
```

The gateway starts on its own once the Secret is there. It scales with load, each replica keeping
its own volume (records not yet delivered, the last known configuration and keys) and a stable
name, so it stays one instance on the Overview. Because there can be several replicas, the
organization's key comes **from the Secret only**: the Settings tab shows it and says so. After
changing the Secret, restart the gateway: `kubectl -n theygent rollout restart statefulset/ai-gateway`.

For developers outside the cluster, expose the `ai-gateway` Service with an Ingress or a load
balancer; in development, `kubectl -n theygent port-forward svc/ai-gateway 8082:8082`.

## The organization's key

Developers billed to the organization reach Anthropic with its key, which the gateway adds in
place of theirs. The key belongs to the gateway alone — it never passes through the control plane
— and it is never shown again once set:

- **From the deployment** — `THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_ORG_API_KEY` in `.env`, Compose or the Kubernetes
  Secret. A key set this way cannot be replaced from the page.
- **From the page** — a single gateway (on a machine, or in Compose) also accepts it on
  **AI Gateway → Settings → Organization's Anthropic key**: your browser sends it straight to the
  gateway, which keeps it in its own state directory.

Until a key is set, requests from org-billed developers are refused (`org_key_not_configured`). A
personal gateway has no organization key: everyone uses their own credential.

## Health

| Endpoint | Answers |
|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | Liveness: `{"status":"ok"}` |
| `GET /readyz` | `200` when ready, `503` while starting or — in team mode — until developers' keys are loaded; with the gateway's id, mode, configuration version and control-plane address |

```bash
curl http://localhost:8082/readyz
```

## Errors the gateway returns

When the gateway itself refuses a request, Claude Code shows the message, and the response carries
an `x-theygent-gateway-error` header naming the reason. Anything else — Anthropic's own errors,
rate limits — comes back exactly as Anthropic sent it.

| Status | Code | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 401 | `gateway_key_missing` | The gateway is in team mode: add your gateway key to the setup ([Set up Claude Code](setup.md)) |
| 401 | `gateway_key_invalid` | The key is unknown or revoked: create a new one on Setup & keys |
| 503 | `gateway_keys_unavailable` | The gateway has not loaded developers' keys yet — it is starting, or cannot reach the control plane and has none saved. Retry shortly; check its service key |
| 401 | `upstream_credential_missing` | You are billed to your own credential and Claude Code sent none: sign in to Claude Code, or set your API key |
| 503 | `org_key_not_configured` | You are billed to the organization, and the gateway has no organization key: an admin sets it |
| 403 | `endpoint_not_allowed` | The organization's key serves Claude Code's model endpoints only |
| 504 | `upstream_timeout` | Anthropic did not answer in time (retryable) |
| 502 | `upstream_unreachable` | The gateway could not reach Anthropic: check its network |

## Where it keeps its data

A gateway keeps a small state directory — `~/.theygent/ai-gateway` on a machine, a volume in
Compose and Kubernetes (`THEYGENT_AI_GATEWAY_STATE_DIR` moves it): the records it has not
delivered yet (so nothing is lost while the control plane is down), the last known configuration,
developers' keys as one-way digests (never the keys themselves), and a stored organization key.
Every file is readable by its owner only.

The control plane keeps each request in detail for 90 days by default (**AI Gateway → Settings →
Request records**; 0 keeps everything). After that, a whole day at a time moves to a compressed
archive in the same database. Reports read archived days from daily totals that keep every
grouping, so no figure changes. Only those days' per-request timelines leave the Sessions tab,
and the card lists each archived day for download. A day's records arrive as JSON lines, one
record each, exactly as the gateway sent it.

## Related pages

- [Environment variables](../reference/environment.md#ai-gateway) — every gateway setting.
- [Set up Claude Code](setup.md) — the client side.
- [Running TheYgent](../getting-started/running.md) — the other services.

Source: https://docs.theygent.ai/latest/import-export/

# Import & export

**Settings → Import / Export** moves an install — or any part of it — between machines as a single zip file. Export packs your agents, runs, traces, chats, MCP servers, RAG sources, and model registrations into one download; import unpacks a bundle on another machine, shows you a preview of exactly what it will create, and only writes after you confirm. Two things never travel in a bundle, by design: **secret values** and **model weights** — the import preview tells you what has to be re-entered or re-downloaded on the target.

You can also export and import a **single agent** as a plain JSON file, straight from the Agents page — see [Drafts & publishing](../building/saving-agents.md#exporting-and-deleting-agents).

## What's in a bundle

The Export card offers seven sections; each maps to a slice of your install:

| Section | What travels |
|---|---|
| **Agents** | Every published agent with **all** its versions (graph + canvas layout), plus your drafts, triggers, and per-agent I/O capture policies. |
| **Runs** | The full run history — status, model, parameters, output, timestamps. |
| **Traces** | Per-run spans and node I/O, plus the audio/image artifacts your runs produced (packed as raw files in the zip). Selecting Traces automatically includes Runs — a trace without its runs would be unreadable. |
| **Chats** | Sessions and their messages, in order. |
| **MCP servers** | Connections and name-keyed MCP server registrations — definitions only. |
| **RAG sources** | Source definitions (name, kind, embedding model, crawl config) — no documents or vectors. |
| **Model registry** | Your model registrations (logical id → binding), the catalog-install provenance needed to re-download weights, and credential **names**. |

!!! warning "What is never in a bundle"
    Bundles carry definitions, never credentials or weights. Specifically excluded, always:

    - **Secret values of any kind** — connection secrets, webhook signing secrets, and MCP env/header *values* (only the key names travel, so the target knows what to ask you for).
    - **API credential values** — the inference plane exports credential *names* only (e.g. `HF_TOKEN`), never values.
    - **Model weights** — registrations re-download their weights on the target, or point at weights you reinstall yourself.
    - **RAG content** — documents, chunks, and vectors stay behind; sources re-ingest on the target.

    There is no way to opt secrets or weights into a bundle. An export zip is safe to store or hand over in the sense that it contains no credential material — but it does contain your prompts, run outputs, and chat history, so treat it with the same care as the install itself.

## Exporting

1. Open **Settings** from the sidebar and switch to the **Import / Export** tab.
2. In the **Export** card, tick the sections you want — **All** is pre-selected. Ticking **Traces** pulls **Runs** along automatically (and unticking Runs drops Traces).
3. Click **Export**. Your browser downloads one file, named like `theygent-export-2026-07-18.zip`.

If an artifact referenced by a trace no longer exists on disk, the export skips it and tells you in a toast — the zip still completes.

!!! note "The zip is assembled in your browser"
    The browser fetches the control-plane sections from `:8080` and the model registry **directly** from your inference plane on `:8081`, then zips them together locally. Registry state never passes through the control plane — the browser is the only place both halves meet, which is why the export lives in the interface rather than behind a single server endpoint.

The curl equivalents fetch the two halves separately. The control plane serves its bundle from `POST /export` (pick any subset of `agents`, `runs`, `traces`, `sessions`, `mcp`, `rag` — an empty or unknown selection is `400 invalid_include`):

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/export \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"include": ["agents", "runs", "traces", "sessions", "mcp", "rag"]}' \
  -o control-plane.json
```

The inference plane serves its registry bundle from `GET /admin/export`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8081/admin/export -o models.json
```

## Importing

1. In the **Import** card, click **Choose file…** and pick a theygent export zip — or a single exported agent `.json`.
2. Read the **preview**: per-section counts plus prominent warnings — how many models will download weights from Hugging Face, how many connections will need credentials re-entered or re-authorized, which MCP servers need env values, which RAG sources need re-crawling or re-uploading, and the credential **names** the source inference plane had (values never travel — re-enter them on the target). **Nothing is written at this point.**
3. Click **Import…** and confirm in the dialog.
4. The report shows what was created, what was skipped, and every warning. Any model weight downloads the import kicked off appear as progress cards in the notification center (bottom-right), exactly like a catalog install.

### Import rules

- **Existing entities are kept, never overwritten.** Anything whose id (or name, for MCP servers) already exists on the target is skipped. That makes an import **safe to re-run** — importing the same bundle twice changes nothing the second time.
- **Content hashes are recomputed by the server.** An imported agent version is validated and re-hashed exactly like a publish; the hash in the file is never trusted. If the target already has the same agent version with *different* content, that version is reported as a `version_conflict` and skipped — the rest of the bundle still imports.
- **One bad entry never aborts the rest.** An invalid agent version, an unparseable row — each is reported in the warnings list while everything else lands.
- **Ids and timestamps are preserved**, so runs, traces, and chats on the new machine correlate exactly like the originals.

### After an import

Because secrets and weights never travel, some things need your attention on the target:

- **Connections** import without their secret — re-enter it (or re-run the OAuth authorization) on the [MCP page](../mcp/index.md) before the connection works.
- **Webhook triggers** import **disabled** and without a signing secret. Set a new secret (`PATCH /triggers/{id}`), then enable the trigger. Schedule triggers import as they were.
- **MCP servers** import with their env/header values empty — open the server's settings and re-enter them.
- **RAG sources** import empty: re-run the crawl, or re-upload the documents.
- **Model weights** re-download automatically for catalog-installed models (watch the notification center). A model that was registered against a local file path with no install provenance is registered anyway but warns `weights_unavailable` — it will fail at first use until you put weights at that path or reinstall it. See [Moving models to another machine](../models/index.md#moving-models-to-another-machine).

The curl equivalents import the two JSON halves the zip contains (the zip itself has no single server endpoint — the browser unpacks it). A body that isn't a bundle is `400 invalid_bundle`; a bundle from a future TheYgent is `400 unsupported_bundle_version`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/import \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @control-plane.json
```

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/admin/import \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @models.json
```

Artifacts (the raw files under `artifacts/` in the zip) restore under their original refs with `PUT /artifacts/{ref}` — a ref that already exists on the target is kept, never overwritten (the response says `created: false`):

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/artifacts/art_01J9ZS3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FA \
  -H 'Content-Type: audio/webm' \
  --data-binary @art_01J9ZS3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FA
```
